newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr worn down by rate rumour mill.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr worn down by rate rumour mill.

text.p: The Australian dollar ended the week at a low ebb as persistent worries about a cut in domestic interest rates frayed market nerves.

The currency came under pressure right from the start after Treasurer Peter Costello, evoking the name of Santa Claus, said there was good reason to expect lower rates both this year and next. The comment, imprecise as it was, fed the market's policy paranoia and prompted profit taking across the board.
But exporter and Japanese retail demand offered a cushion, and dealers feared a prolonged bout of consolidation lay ahead until the rate outlook here and in the U.S. was clarified.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had sagged to US$0.7896/01 from an early US$0.7906/11 and US$0.7919/24 late here Thursday, which made the week's US$0.7964 high look like an abberation.

Interim support was seen at US$0.7885 and a break of last week's low of US$0.7855 would turn the fragile mood much more bearish, dealers said. Resistance was pegged at US$0.7920 and the currency needed to regain US$0.7945 at least to restore some confidence to the uptrend.
The dollar was down at 88.02/12 yen from 88.47/57 Thursday, although that was a relatively robust performance given it was not far from the four year high of 89.21 hit on Wednesday.
In trade weighted terms the dollar waned to 58.3 from 58.7, but again was not that far away from a five year high of 59.0.

Traders said Japanese investors were still keen on higher yielding offshore assets now that the second half of their financial year had begun and rates there looked certain to remain at record lows until well into 1997.
The Reserve Bank's decision not to cut domestic rates in the wake of its monthly board meeting Tuesday meant that, for the moment at least, A$ assets were included on their shopping list.
And there was growing speculation the Federal Reserve might be able to see out the year without having to tighten policy.
This was important for the local currency as a hike in U.S. rates would have further trimmed its yield advantage and perhaps turned Japanese investors elsewhere.
However, the steady rate view depended crucially on tonight's U.S. payrolls report for September.
"Jobs growth needs to slow to an average 140,000-150,000 a month to support this new optimism on rates," said Richard Gibbs, an international economist at Macquarie Bank.
Median forecasts are for payrolls to rise 166,000, down from 250,000 in August, and there was much talk in bond circles it could be a bit weaker than that.
Gibbs cautioned that this may be wishful thinking, having just been on a client trip to the U.S. where he was impressed by the strength of the labour market, particularly in the mid-west.
"Basic service markets, like cleaning, are booming while the professional end is having to hike salaries to keep workers from being poached," Gibbs said.
He noted that there had even been a sharp rise in employment growth for black males in the 20-30 year age group, a sector of the population prone to high rates of long term unemployment.
"I suspect the risk for payrolls is on the upside and we haven't heard the last of a Fed tightening this year," he said.
There were no domestic data to provide a countervailing influence so the local dollar could be vulnerable to profit taking if Gibbs' suspicions proved correct.

On the domestic front the market was assuming, rightly or not, that the Reserve Bank board would wait to see if Q3 consumer price and wages data confirmed their belief inflation was heading lower over the next year before easing policy.
Australian employment figures for September on Thursday might expand on the risk of a rate cut, especially if the notoriously volatile figures were outside forecasts.
